*Note of 29 October 2026: the numbers in this summary are those of the 11-species runs of 12 and 13 October. The roster for the first version of the Monitor has 14 species (28 October); a clean run recomputes everything, and the pipeline has meanwhile been extended with one study area for all inputs, complete predictor layers and a connector that fills the folder the Monitor reads. This summary has not been changed otherwise.*

The birdMonitor modelling pipeline turns bird records and environmental data into yearly maps and national indices for 11 species (2005-2025), with confidence intervals on everything, all within Germany's borders.

## At a glance

- **A model pipeline** combines three spatial scales (climate 50 km, landscape 1 km, habitat 200 m) for 11 species and 21 years, following the pre-print Wiedenroth et al. method.
- **Honest accuracy.** The weights that combine the scales are trained and tested on predictions the models did not see, which differs from the original  method, but is likely more robust.
- **Uncertainty throughout.** A spatial bootstrap with 50 replicates of the models gives an interval for every map, change map, trend and index, including the regional indices on 10, 20 and 50 km grids.
- **An ensemble of five algorithms (the "big 5"),** with its own uncertainty. It is more accurate than the single algorithm and shows a stronger decline.

## What the results show so far

Within Germany, the model-based combined index of the 11 species stands at 95.6 in 2025 (2005 = 100), a decline of about 4%, and nine of the 11 species are below their 2005 level in the main model; for eight of them the 90% interval of the replicates lies entirely below 100. The 90% interval from 50 model replicates runs from 94.0 to 98.2, so the decline is small but its direction does not depend on the training data. These are the results with one algorithm (BRT only).

With the big 5, the combined index is lower: 93.3 in 2025 for the main model, with a 90% interval from 91.5 to 95.7 (25 replicates, mean 93.5). The two intervals overlap only between 94.0 and 95.7, so the big 5 shows a stronger decline than the single algorithm. The big 5 is also more accurate: its AUC is higher than that of the BRT in 31 of 33 combinations of species and scale (on average by 0.019).

| Species | BRT only: main model | BRT only: 90% interval (50 replicates) | Big 5: main model | Big 5: 90% interval (25 replicates) |

| Saxicola rubetra | 82.7 | 75.2 to 92.7 | 77.1 | 70.0 to 88.5 |
| Vanellus vanellus | 90.8 | 90.2 to 95.6 | 92.6 | 90.2 to 95.5 |
| Perdix perdix | 91.1 | 84.7 to 100.0 | 84.1 | 77.4 to 98.3 |
| Alauda arvensis | 94.9 | 93.7 to 95.8 | 94.3 | 93.3 to 95.0 |
| Anthus pratensis | 95.7 | 84.6 to 97.2 | 92.1 | 86.0 to 94.3 |
| Lanius collurio | 97.3 | 96.0 to 99.5 | 95.5 | 89.8 to 97.7 |
| Emberiza citrinella | 97.4 | 96.7 to 98.0 | 97.6 | 96.6 to 97.8 |
| Buteo buteo | 97.7 | 97.5 to 98.7 | 97.8 | 97.3 to 98.3 |
| Sturnus vulgaris | 98.8 | 98.3 to 99.2 | 98.9 | 98.7 to 99.2 |
| Emberiza calandra | 102.6 | 97.2 to 118.8 | 96.8 | 91.7 to 97.8 |
| Lullula arborea | 104.5 | 98.7 to 109.8 | 102.2 | 93.4 to 106.0 |
| **Combined index** | **95.6** | **94.0 to 98.2** | **93.3** | **91.5 to 95.7** |

The biggest differences between the two runs are Emberiza calandra (a slight increase with one algorithm, a decline with the big 5, whose interval does not contain 100), Perdix perdix and Lanius collurio. For Perdix perdix, 9 of the 50 replicates of the single-algorithm run have a constant map (index 100 in every year), because the model found no usable signal in those resamples, which is why the upper end of that interval is 100. We kept them and will report a second interval without them after the meeting; the same check is still to be done for the big 5.

Two cautions go with every number. The maps for 2005-2021 are a hindcast, because the habitat model learns from 2022-2025 data only, so the series shows how the landscape changed under fixed habitat preferences, not how the birds changed. And the intervals describe model uncertainty from the training data, not the uncertainty of counts in the field.

## How far the uncertainty reaches

The intervals show how much each result would change if the models had been trained on different data, and they cover every product we deliver.

- **Covered:** the sampling of the training data at all three scales, the weights that combine the scales, and everything derived from them: maps, change, trend, species and combined indices, regional indices, richness and turnover. With the big 5, the choice of algorithm is covered too.
- **Not covered:** errors in the environmental layers, tuning of model settings, biases in how the birds were surveyed, the randomness of the thinning of the records, and whether habitat preferences were the same before 2022.
- **How to read an interval:** it is a 90% range of the model result, not a range for what an observer would count in the field, and it is based on 25 to 50 replicates. It is an approximate interval: the weak points of the bootstrap and the plan to check them are in the improvements list.
